item.title: Translations, Screenplays, and Watered-Down Stoicism
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

What makes a good translation? Kang defended the translation and continued working with Smith. Classicist Emily Wilson tackles that and other literary debates in Crossing the Wine-Dark Sea: Journeys Through Ancient Literature (Bookshop \| Amazon), drawing on her acclaimed translations of The Odyssey (Bookshop \| Amazon) and The Iliad (Bookshop \| Amazon). She demonstrates what works and what doesn’t in translations of Sappho as social mores change, asks why tech bros love watered-down stoicism, and along the way invokes everyone from Cicero to Cardi B. In fact, Wilson’s no stranger to pop culture, as evidenced by her scorching essay declaring that Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster film suffered from scriptwriting that was, she declared, “abysmal.” This is part of a complete episode.

Transcript of “Emily Wilson on Translating Sappho, Why Tech Bros Love Watered-Down Stoicism, and the Nolan Film Script”

You’re listening to A Way with Words, the show about language and how we use it.

I’m Grant Barrett.

And I’m Martha Barnette.

In 2016, South Korean writer Hong Kong won the International Booker Prize for her novel, The Vegetarian, and so did Smith, who translated the novel into English.

The prize money was divided equally between them, but the award wasn’t without controversy.

Some Korean readers and scholars pointed to mistranslations in places where Smith took liberties with the author’s prose.

And they even questioned whether Smith, who had begun learning Korean just a few years before, really knew the language well enough to render the text responsibly.

The novelist rejected the idea that Smith’s translation had fundamentally betrayed the original, and in fact, the two of them went on to collaborate on other books, all of which raises a question that translators have been arguing about for 2,000.

What exactly makes a good translation?

Is it better to use your own creativity to convey a sense of what the author is saying, or is a word-for-word translation superior?

Should a translator use perfectly styled English prose, or is it better to try to preserve a bit of the foreignness of the first language?

Well, in a bracing collection of new essays, classicist Emily Wilson tackles these questions and a whole lot more.

Her book is called Crossing the Wine Dark Sea, Journeys through Ancient Literature.

Wilson is the acclaimed translator of both the Iliad and the Odyssey, and she made headlines earlier this year for a scorching essay about Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster movie.

She called the scriptwriting abysmal.

Well, she’s quite opinionated in this book as well, but the book is a delight to read because she always backs up those strong opinions in lively, interesting ways.

In fact, she invokes everyone from Cicero to Cardi B.

She examines lots of translations showing what works and what doesn’t and how every translation involves compromise.

Her essays involve a lot of other topics as well, like how translations of Sappho have changed over time and why so many tech bros now find a watered down, cherry picked version of ancient Greek stoicism so appealing.

So it’s this invigorating book that helps you engage with ancient literature in the ancient world without idealizing them.

It’s called Crossing the Journeys Through Ancient Literature by classicist Emily Wilson.

I absolutely have to read that because I have a problem where I love international literature, not written in English, but I know that the translations are faulty just because what I know about translations and it and it bothers me that I can’t get closer to the author’s original voice and intent and that I have to have this this mediator.

You know?

Right.

It’s just as a as a big reader, it it it pains me that I can’t know the author like they need to be known.

Right.

We’d love to hear your opinions on translation, whether it’s a favorite translations or one that you don’t really care for very much.

If you just wanna tell us about what’s on your bookshelf or next to the bed that you read before nodding off, call or text toll-free from The US and Canada, (877-929-9673, or go to our website where you’ll find a lot of ways to reach us and all of our past episodes at no charge.

item.title: alongside
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

A few months ago, an American friend of my spouse asked him to ask me: "Why is everyone suddenly saying alongside?" I hadn't noticed it at that point, but once he'd mentioned it, I felt surrounded by alongside.

As this Google Books ngram shows, the word has taken off in the 21st century:

Separating out the British and American books, we can see that this is a British-led trend.

Alongside climbed in British usage throughout the 20th century. American English suddenly decided to (orig. AmE) play catch-up in the 21st century.

This trend is observable in other corpora too. The News on the Web corpus, for example, shows more than double the rate of alongside in British news sources versus American ones.

And within the US News data, the rise of alongside has sped up since 2020.

Among(st) the prepositions, alongside is a relative (orig. AmE) newbie. In the OED, where it's marked as "originally nautical," its first citation is from 1704; its definition: "In a position parallel to; side by side with; close to the side of; next to, beside." So the examples are about boats positioned next to other boats or docks, etc. It seems to have gradually moved onto land, especially in the UK, in the 19th century.

So why have Americans suddenly (orig. AmE) taken a shine to alongside? Why is it more attractive than along or beside or next to? Wondering whether there was a trend toward(s) longer, British prepositions, I tried comparing it to amongst. But the more-BrE amongst seems to have peaked in AmE about 12 years ago:

In 2013, the online magazine Slate published an article by Ben Yagoda about Americans saying amongst instead of among. Perhaps once people were talking about the "British invasion" of amongst, Americans became more self-conscious about it. If Ben published an article about alongside, could that change its fortunes?

Having had alongside pointed out to me, I'm now self-conscious about using it. But this blog gives us a record of me using it:

- "BrE has kerb for the edging alongside a road" (curb/kerb, May 2020)

- "British pigs in blankets are small sausages wrapped in bacon (and cooked!). They are delicious. They're traditionally served alongside turkey as part of Christmas dinner." (pigs in blankets, Feb 2020)

- "I've seen a lot of "down with grammar!" messages, often alongside 'learning should be fun!'" (grammar is not the enemy, May 2016)

So, what do you think: do I sound Britified when I say such things, or is alongside completely international now?

***

PS: Searching for commentary about alongside, I found some concern about the use of alongside with. Further (orig. BrE) rooting around in the corpora, though, show that alongside with is a tiny proportion of alongside usages (0.7 per million words in AmE, 0.8 per million words in BrE in the NOW corpus).

Source: Separated by a Common Language | Published: 2026-03-21 23:42 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.description:

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

Joe from Madison, Wisconsin, remembers his Romanian-born grandmother recounting the story of a Depression-era neighbor, a tailor with eight children, who answered “How are you?” with a Yiddish phrase that means I touch the wall and I chew the earth. This saying combines two established expressions: touch the wall, which means “to grope blindly and struggle without success,” and chew the earth, which can mean “to be dirt poor, starving, humiliated, or simply dead and buried.” The first likely echoes a passage in the biblical Book of Isaiah about groping for the wall like a blind person. Other Yiddish-inspired euphemisms for dying include stretch out your feet, close an eye, and the darkly comic lie in the ground and bake bagels. This is part of a complete episode.

item.title: French Origin of “Dishabille” for Being Underdressed
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

Janet from Concord, New Hampshire, remembers her mother in the 1950s using it to indicate she wasn’t appropriately dressed for an unexpected outing or visitor, declaring, I’m not ready—I’m in my dishabille. The word comes from French déshabillé and turns up mostly in literary and fashion texts, where it means “underdressed,” “nearly nude,” or simply “not dressed for the occasion.” In the 18th century, dishabille also denoted a style of flowing garments, as opposed to the stiff corsets and layered public gowns of the time. This is part of a complete episode.

Transcript of “The French Origin of “Dishabille” for Being Underdressed”

Hello.

You have A Way with Words.

Hi.

This is Janet from Concord, New Hampshire.

Thank you for taking my call.

We’re glad to have you, Janet.

What’s on your mind?

Well, from the time I was a child back in the nineteen fifties, my mother used a word I’ve never heard anyone else in our family or anywhere else use, and that was the word.

My mother was always careful to be appropriately dressed for whatever occasion.

For example, if she was in her pajamas or she was casually dressed for a day at home and we had a surprise opportunity to go out for ice cream or another opportunity or someone called and they were gonna come by, she might say, I’m not ready.

I’m in my dish a deal.

And that meant she wasn’t appropriate dress for the occasion, and we all knew that meant it’s gonna take some time because she was gonna change her clothes before we did whatever the opportunity was.

Mhmm.

Mhmm.

And it’s a fairly efficient word to just say disable to mean all of that.

So I’m looking forward to hearing your wisdom where that word came from and if it was ever widely used?

Yeah.

That’s a lot of good questions there.

And I think your story perfectly nails some aspects of the word.

I’m gonna spell this.

It’s d I s h a b I l l e.

And I think most people can tell by the look of that word that it…

It’s got a French origin.

Martha, how do you pronounce that word?

Well, I will tell you that for the longest time, I pronounce it the way Janet does, Deshabil.

Yeah.

Deshabil.

So that’s, like, the absolutely most English-sounding thing ever.

Right?

Yes.

Yes.

But later in life, I I ran across the pronunciation and started pronouncing it disabile.

Disabile.

Yeah.

Something like that.

Disabile.

So it comes from French.

And, basically, you’ll see it…

The pronunciations vary from very French sounding to very English sounding.

But the French word is actually spelled a little different.

It’s d e with an acute accent, s h a b I l l e, with another e, with an acute accent.

It sounds something a des habillers, instead of des chabels.

So most of the pronunciations that people use for the word English speaking world are based on seeing it in print, which ties into how it’s most often used, is in literary or fashion texts.

It’s not something that’s usually said aloud.

It’s most often…

That’s a showy word that a writer might use to make a point.

And it does mean…

To mean not appropriately dressed, but it also can mean undressed or in the…

Historically, there was a style of dress called the Des Avier in the eighteenth century and involved these kind of flowing garments that you would wear in private.

They contrast it with the very strict like corsetry and layered gowns that you might wear in public.

So there’s many centuries of kind of changing nuances for this work, but in general, it’s all about not having the right clothes on for the place that you’re in, or having no clothes at all, because it can be nearly nude, depending on the context.

That was never my mother.

There’s another layer to this too, which I want to bring up here, Janet.

And this is this thing that French still has going on after so many centuries of French and English commingling and the two cultures kind of intertwined, that French still has this ability to make the most ordinary things sound provocative or hyphaluten, so to speak, or maybe even sensual.

Right?

This idea that French is the classier, more prestige language is something that English just cannot shake, particularly when it comes to fashion and appearance.

You.

It’s a great treat, and it’s a great treat to speak with you both.

Oh, It’s a treat to speak with you, Jen.

Yeah, Jen.

Alright.

Thanks for sharing.

Thanks.

Bye-bye.

Bye-bye.

item.title: Are these words misspelled/misspelt most?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

The people at WordUnscrambler.pro sent me a list of "the most misspelled (BrE misspelt*) words" for the UK.

But I first have to gripe a bit. Here's the methodology:

We analyzed Jan 1, 2025 - Dec 17, 2025 search data from Google Trends for "How do you spell" and "How to spell".

That's not a method for discovering the "most misspelled words." That's a method for discovering the most looked-up spellings. This is the kind of (BrE) jiggery-pokery makes me hate headlines. If you think to look up a word, then you might be insecure or curious about its spelling. But that's keeping you from misspelling it. I'm betting that when they're not looking up spellings like these, those people are out in the world (like the rest of us) are confidently spelling accommodation with one m and letting spellcheck catch it for them (or not).

Nevertheless, the WU.pro folks showed admirable linguistic sensitivity in not declaring the Americanisms on the list "misspelled." Instead, they note repeatedly that both the US and UK variants "are correct".

United Kingdom's most misspelled words queried spellings:

1. Colour - 109 200 searches - Both colour and color are correct.

2. Favourite - 82 900 searches - Both favourite and favorite are correct.

3. License - 59 000 searches.

4. Diarrhoea - 58 700 searches - Both diarrhoea and diarrhea are correct.

5. Jewellery - 56 400 searches.

6. Definitely - 53 000 searches.

7. Auntie - 50 400 searches - Both auntie and aunty are correct.

8. Weird - 48 000 searches.

9. Business - 46 800 searches.

10. Behaviour - 40 800 searches - Both behaviour and behavior are correct.

11. Neighbour - 39 600 searches - Both neighbour and neighbor are correct.

12. Country - 29 000 searches.

13. Queue - 22 800 searches.

14. Gorgeous - 22 600 searches.

15. Necessary - 23 000 searches.

I've added the blue to show which ones are also on the US top 10, which I've copied at the bottom of this post.† (Not sure why the UK got a top 15 and the US a top 10. Nor why necessary has more searches but is lower on the list than queue.)

Some of these are definitely difficult—others, like country, surprised me. But let's have a little look at whether people do misspell them, using the Corpus of Global Web-Based English. (I'm using that one even though it's 13 years old now because web-based English is more likely to include misspellings than the published writing in other comparative corpora.) I won't try to cover all of them, just the ones that strike me as transatlantically interesting.

Postscript : On the same day as I wrote this post, another company released its (much better) analysis of British misspellings. See the bottom of this post for more on that.

US/UK variants

-or/-our

In that vein, the following graph shows that there's probably more AmE writing on UK websites than BrE writing on AmE websites—which is not so surprising, since there are presumably about 5 times more US than UK writers on the internet and text from American wire services and other companies might be reprinted wholesale on UK sites.

But the other thing to take from the our/or chart is: Canadian spelling is in crisis. The (standard Canadian) -our spellings only just outnumber the -or ones. Meanwhile, the Canadian Prime Minister recently got into trouble for using British -ise spellings that are not traditionally Canadian.

licence/license

License is a tricky one because it's the correct spelling for BrE, when it is a verb. But it is licence in BrE when it is a noun (s in AmE for both). The first chart here shows a lot of (incorrect for BrE) license as a noun in the GB corpus—but that will, again, be partly due to American writing on British websites, rather than British writers misspelling it. It's hard to know how much each factor contributes.

I was surprised not to see practice/practise on the UK misspelling list. You can read more about that at an older post, if you'd like to.

Diarrhea/diarrhoea

This one seems to have little to do with US/UK confusion. Diarrh(o)ea is just difficult and unpleasant for everyone. And personal: everybody's misspelling it their own ways:

(The crossed-out ones are names that happened to be caught on my search for "diarr*a". I don't envy them their diarr-a names.)

jewellery/jewelry

The later jewellery spelling seems to have derived from jeweller + y ('the stuff that the jeweller makes'—analogous to pottery) while jewelry derives from jewel+ry ('products created from jewels'—analogous to pastry, balladry). In 1901, the OED commented (about BrE usage):

In commercial use commonly spelt jewellery; the form jewelry is more rhetorical and poetic, and unassociated with the jeweller. But the pronunciation with three syllables is usual even with the former spelling.

So, we might consider jewelry to be AmE and old-fashioned BrE.

Words that are just hard to spell

Weird

It's been my perception that weird is more a problem in UK spelling, and GloWbE bears that out a little bit, with wierd a greater proportion of the UK forms (about 3%) than the US (about 2%):

country

queue

The word is much more common in BrE, but hard to spell everywhere. And yet, people seem to mostly get it right. Leaving off the final e sometimes happens, but really not much:

I'd expected to find the word spelled like its homonyms cue and Q, but there aren't many such misspellings. For the following chart, I searched for queue, queu, que, Q and cue, but none of the queu spellings showed up in the 'in a' phrasing:

The Q spelling might be an abbreviation, rather than a misspelling. But it's striking that the cue homonym is absent from the British entirely. These people know a queue's a queue.

I'm going to leave it there! But feel free to comment on these or the other words on the lists.

Footnotes…

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

Holly of Madison, Wisconsin, notes that there are four unique points on the planet where the 90-degree and 45-degree lines of longitude and latitude meet. She’s visited the most accessible one, located in Wisconsin’s Marathon County. There a geographical marker designates the spot and visitors can pick up an official medallion in nearby Wausau. The two southern points lie deep in the ocean, and the northeastern one is somewhere in remote China. These four spots where a 45-degree latitude line meets a 90-degree longitude line are referred to in several ways, including 45×90 points, degree confluences, and quarter hemispheric centers. This is part of a complete episode.

What’s time to a hog? Steve in Virginia Beach, Virginia, says his 95-year-old Dutch mother-in-law in Holland, Michigan, was fond of asking that question, but Steve never got a good explanation as to its meaning or origin. What’s time to a hog? is the punchline of a joke that comes in several versions, one of many clever peasant tales that feature wise country folk who outsmart visitors from the city. In this case, a city slicker tells a farmer how to fatten hogs faster, and the farmer just shrugs and responds with that question. What’s time to a hog? can also mean “What’s the hurry?” or “Take your time.” Or you can use the phrase to gently chide someone who’s dawdling. This is part of a complete episode.
